reflection_text.2:
The potential outcomes set up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $m(X)=E[Y_0|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$. The population regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the mean difference, so the $D$ coefficient is strictly positive. This is uncontroversial.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)+h(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ can be negative and arbitrarily large in magnitude because $P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ can be decreasing in $X$ while $m(X)$ is increasing in $X$. Example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The simple OLS coefficient $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ is therefore not sign protected. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 agree.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)=D-a-bX$ with $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[r]=E[rX]=0$. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The second term is the weighted average of the positive $h(X)$ but the first term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linear partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$. Because no parametric form for $m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is imposed, $m(X)$ can be chosen to be oppositely correlated with $r(X)$ to make the covariance arbitrarily negative. 

The weighted-average representation $ \beta_D=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ holds for the residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for non-parametric partialling out of $X$, not for the linear projection $D-a-bX$ used in OLS. With a non-linear $p(X)$, $\tilde D\neq D-E[D|X]$ and the $m(X)$ term survives. Explicit counter-examples with $p(X)=X^2$ or $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $m(X)= -K\,r(X)$ give $\beta_D<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for all $X$. This is the linear Simpson reversal noted by colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8.

Hence positivity of $\tau_i>0$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. The marginal regression under conditional randomisation can flip, and the linear regression with a linear control for $X$ can also flip because OLS is a linear projection, not the conditional mean. The claim that Case 3 is guaranteed positive rests on conflating $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$. 

Current belief: only Case 1 must be positive. That is option A. Colleagues arguing for E rely on the non-linear residual or on an implicit linearity assumption on $m(X)$ and $p(X)$, which is excluded by “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”.
reflection_text.4:
The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional randomisation $E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. The population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$, so the coefficient is strictly positive. Agreed by all.

Case 2. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ marginally. The marginal OLS coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)+h(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$. The $h$ term is positive but the selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ is increasing. Classic Simpson reversal e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$. So the sign is not guaranteed.

Case 3. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ and we run the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$. With the Frisch–Waugh residual $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, $\beta={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$. 
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)]+{\rm Cov}(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X])$
$=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)h(X),\,w(X)\big)$
where $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. The first term is $>0$. The second term is the linear covariance of $E[Y|X]$ with the part of $p(X)$ not linearly explained by $X$. With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$, $h(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ this second term can be made arbitrarily negative. Choosing $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$ with $K$ large, or e.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$, gives $\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$. The same effect is obtained with $p(X)=X^{2}$ and $m_{0}(X)=-K\big(X^{2}-X+1/6\big)$.

Hence the population linear coefficient is a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional effects only when the residual is $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. under non-parametric control for $X$. With a linear control the linear projection can reverse sign because the linear approximation to $m_{0}(X)$ and $p(X)$ need not preserve the monotone conditional relationship.

The disagreement in round 0 is exactly this: Colleagues 1,12,6,7,9 treat the OLS coefficient after adding $X$ as a positive weighted average of $h(X)$, essentially using $E[\tilde D|X]=0$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 point out the $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\neq0$ term and give explicit counterexamples where the linear coefficient is negative despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$.

Given the instruction not to make parametric assumptions beyond positivity of $\tau$, the linear projection is not sign-preserving. The only guaranteed sign is unconditional randomisation.

Current belief: positivity guaranteed only in Case 1. Case 2 fails by selection on $X$, Case 3 fails by linear approximation error when $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ are non-linear in $X$. Unresolved nuance is the distinction between the non-parametric partial effect $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ and the linear OLS coefficient.
reflection_text.10:
The core set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ and the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$. The marginal regression coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is a selection bias because $P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ can be monotone opposite to $m_0$. With $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ we get $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$. So sign not guaranteed. All colleagues agree.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$. The Frisch-Waugh coefficient is $\beta_D=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}(D)=D-a-bX$.
Writing $p(X)=E[D|X]$,
$E[Y\tilde D]=E[(m_0(X)+h(X)p(X))(p(X)-a-bX)]+E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]$.
Hence
$\beta_D=
\frac{E[(m_0(X)+h(X)p(X))(p(X)-a-bX)]+E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}
     {E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+E[(p(X)-a-bX)^2] }$.
The second numerator term is $>0$ and is a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$. The first numerator term is $\operatorname{Cov}\big(m_0(X)+h(X)p(X),\,p(X)-a-bX\big)$ and can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing $m_0$ or $p$ non-linear in $X$. With non-parametric control $\tilde D^*=D-p(X)$ the coefficient would be $E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]/E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$. With only a linear control the residual $p(X)-a-bX$ remains correlated with $m_0(X)$, so the linear projection can flip sign.

Colleagues 1,12,6,7,9 claim linear control preserves sign by a weighted average of $h(X)$; they effectively treat $\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}(D)=E[D|X]$ . Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 give explicit counter-examples where $p(X)$ is non-linear, e.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $m_0(X)=-K(p(X)-E[p])$, $h\equiv1$, giving $\beta_D\propto1-K<0$. That is valid under no parametric restriction on $m_0$ and $p$.

Given the instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the linear projection is not guaranteed to preserve the sign. The only guaranteed positive population coefficient is the unconditionally randomised mean difference.

Current belief: positivity is forced only in Case 1, i.e. A. Only Case 1. Case 2 can be negative by selection on $X$, Case 3 can be negative by the linear-approximation Simpson reversal even with conditional randomisation. Unresolved nuance is whether the problem intends the “partial effect” interpretation with non-parametric control; under that interpretation Cases 1 and 3 would be positive, but under strict OLS linearity the correct guarantee is Case 1 alone.
reflection_text.8:
The maintained potential outcomes model is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s., i.e. $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$. The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]=E[Y_1]$, $E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_0]$ and 
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau]>0$. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ marginally. 
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The second term is the selection bias on $X$. With $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing in $X$ the marginal mean difference can be made negative, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. Sign is not guaranteed. This is agreed on all sides.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and the regression is $Y\sim1+D+X$. 
Conditional on $X$, $Cov(D,Y\mid X)=Var(D\mid X)h(X)>0$. With the non-linear residual $D-E[D\mid X]$,
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]>0$, so the $L^2$ projection on the sigma-field generated by $X$ preserves sign. The OLS projection uses the linear residual $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D\mid X]$. Hence

$\beta_D= Cov(\tilde D,Y)/Var(\tilde D)=Cov(\tilde D,m_0(X))/Var(\tilde D)+E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/Var(\tilde D)$

up to linearisation. The first term is $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ with $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
By choosing $m_0(X)=-K\,w(X)$ and $h(X)>0$ fixed, $Cov(\tilde D,Y)$ can be made arbitrarily negative. Discrete counter-examples with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $m_0=-K w$, $h\equiv1$ give $\beta_D=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$. The same mechanism is $p(X)=X^2$ non-linear in $X$ with $m_0$ chosen orthogonal to $1,X$ but negatively correlated with the linear residual of $p$.

Hence under no parametric restriction on $m_0(X)$ and $p(X)$ the linear coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ can be negative despite pointwise positive conditional effects. The claim that $\beta_D=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]$ holds only for the residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, i.e. for non-parametric control of $X$, not for the linear control $1,X$. 

Colleagues 1,6,7,9,12, E-advocates, assume the linear projection coincides with the conditional expectation residual. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 give the non-linear $p(X)$ / $m_0(X)$ counter-examples showing sign reversal for the linear OLS coefficient. With the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ the linear projection case is not sign-preserving.

So far the only case in which positivity of $\tau_i>0$ forces a positive population OLS coefficient is unconditional randomisation, Case 1. Case 2 is a classic Simpson reversal, and Case 3 can also reverse sign because of linear approximation error when $E[D\mid X]$ or $E[Y_0\mid X]$ is non-linear in $X$. Unresolved nuance is the distinction between non-parametric control of $X$ vs linear control $1+D+X$, which explains the split between E and A camps. Current best reading is A. Only Case 1.

reflection_text.6:
The maintained structure is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Unconditional randomisation gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$.
The OLS slope is the ATE and positivity of $\tau_i$ forces positivity. No disagreement.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while $m_0(X)$ is increasing. Example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<E[Y\mid D=0]=90$. So the marginal regression $Y\sim1+D$ can be negative despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s. Simpson reversal. This is agreed by the majority; the claim that the marginal coefficient remains positive under conditional randomisation is incorrect.

Case 3: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_D D+\gamma X+u$ is used. 
The conditional mean is increasing in $D$ for every $X$, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=h(X)>0$. 
The non-parametric Frisch-Waugh residual $D-p(X)$ satisfies
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of the $h(X)>0$.
The OLS coefficient, however, uses the linear residual $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$,
$\beta_D={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
Because ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$ is only the linear projection of $p(X)$ on $1,X$, 
$E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-a-bX\neq0$ in general. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)E[D\tilde D\mid X]]+E[m_0(X)\tilde D]$
and the term $E[m_0(X)\tilde D]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $m_0(X)$ be anti-correlated with the linear residual of $p(X)$. 
With non-linear $p(X)$ e.g. $p(X)=X^2$ on $[0,1]$ and $m_0(X)=-K\big(p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ the linear coefficient can be driven negative while $h(X)>0$ a.s. Hence the linear projection does not preserve the sign without a linearity restriction on $m_0$ and $p$. 

This is the source of disagreement in the round: colleagues 1,6,7,9,12, E., argue the sign is preserved after controlling for $X$, effectively using the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 point out the OLS residual is linear, and give explicit counter-examples where $\beta_D<0$ under conditional randomisation.

No parametric assumptions beyond binary $D$ and continuous $Y$ are allowed, so $E[Y_0\mid X]$ and $p(X)$ can be arbitrarily non-linear. Under that maintained non-parametric freedom, positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

Current belief: Case 1 must be positive; Case 2 can be negative; Case 3 can be negative for a linear regression of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. Hence only Case 1 is sign- guaranteed. Unresolved tension is the distinction between a linear control and a non-parametric control for $X$, which drives the split between the E and A camps.

reflection_text.9:
The setup is potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., with $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$, $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, under $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ unconditionally. Then
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The OLS slope in $Y\sim1+D$ is exactly the mean difference, so the population coefficient is strictly positive. Unconditional randomisation is forced positive.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D$ is in general dependent on $X$. 
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)+h(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The two expectations are under $P(X\mid D=1)$ vs $P(X\mid D=0)$, which differ when $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ is non-constant. With $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(x)$ increasing and $p(x)$ decreasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $Y_{0}=100X$, one gets $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<E[Y\mid D=0]=90$ despite $\tau>0$ a.s. The marginal $D\sim Y$ coefficient can be negative; sign is not guaranteed.

Case 3. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the regression is the linear projection $Y$ on $1,D,X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$. Then $E[\tilde D\mid X]=0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D\mid X)\big]
=E\big[E[\tau\mid X]E[D(D-\Pi_{1,X}D)\mid X]\big]$.
Now $E[D(D-\Pi_{1,X}D)\mid X]=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)+E[D\mid X]\big(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D\big)$.
The term $E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. Hence
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\!\left[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\right]
+E\!\left[h(X)E[D\mid X]\big(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D\big)\right]
+E\!\left[m_{0}(X)\big(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D\big)\right]$.
The first term is $>0$, but the last two involve the covariance of $m_{0}(X)$ and $h(X)E[D\mid X]$ with the linear projection error of $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$. With a non-linear $p(X)$ this error is non-zero and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$. Explicit counterexamples with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $m_{0}(X)=-K\,\operatorname{Res}_{p}(X)$, $h\equiv1$ give $\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ although $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$. Thus the best linear approximation to $m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ can have a negative $D$ loading despite pointwise positive conditional effects.

Hence under the stated non-parametric conditions the sign is forced only by unconditional randomisation. The marginal regression under conditional randomisation can flip by selection on $X$, and the linear $1+D+X$ projection can also flip by Simpson-type non-linearity of $E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and $p(X)$. The claim that Case 3 is always positive requires $\Pi_{1,X}D=E[D\mid X]$, i.e. linearity of the propensity in $X$, which is a parametric restriction not allowed.

Current belief: positivity is guaranteed only in Case 1. Cases 2 and 3 are not guaranteed. The split in the room between A and E stems exactly from whether the linear projection is assumed to coincide with the conditional expectation; strictly non-parametric it does not.
reflection_text.11:
The maintained model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$. The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ $\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is guaranteed positive.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The conditional gain $h(X)>0$ is positive for every $X$ but the selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when $p(X)=E[D|X]$ is decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ is increasing in $X$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$. So the crude OLS slope can be negative. Agreement on this.

Case 3: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $Y$ is projected on $1,D,X$.
Write $D=p(X)+\eta$, $E[\eta|X]=0$. The linear residual used by OLS is 
$\tilde D=D-a-bX=(p(X)-a-bX)+\eta$ with $a=E[D]$, $b$ the linear regression coefficient of $D$ on $X$. Then

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[r_{p}(X)E[Y|X]\big]+E\big[h(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big]$,

where $r_{p}(X)=p(X)-a-bX$ is the part of $p(X)$ orthogonal to $1,X$ linearly. The second term is $>0$, but the first term $E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]+E[r_{p}(X)p(X)h(X)]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by a non-linear $p(X)$ and a non-linear $m(X)$ chosen anti-correlated with $r_{p}(X)$. In particular $E[r_{p}(X)E[Y|X]]$ is the linear covariance of the baseline mean function with the non-linear part of the propensity score. With $X=0,1,2$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $r_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, and $m(X)=-K\,r_{p}(X)$, $\tau\equiv1$, the OLS coefficient is $\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ even though $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$. 

The common mistake in the deliberation is to replace the linear residual $\tilde D$ by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. With the non-parametric residual $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$, which would guarantee positivity, but that is the coefficient from the (infeasible) regression on $1,D$ and the non-parametric function of $X$, not the linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$. No parametric linearity of $m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is allowed.

Hence positivity of $\tau_i$ for all $i$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can both be signed reversed by non-linear dependence of $p(X)$ on $X$ and of $E[Y_{0}|X]$ on $X$.

Current belief: Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive, i.e. answer A. Disagreement with colleagues 1,6,7,9,12 who claim Case 3 is guaranteed; they conflate linear projection with non-parametric partialling out.

4.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s.,

$$
E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad 
E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0 .
$$

* Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$
and for a binary $D$ the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly this mean
difference. Unconditional randomisation therefore preserves the sign.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$
The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be
arbitrarily negative when $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while
$m_{0}(X)$ is increasing.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  
Hence the crude OLS $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ is not sign-preserved.

* Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$.
Write $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ with
$w(X)=E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX$.
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]
+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)] .
$$
The first term is $>0$. The term $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ is the linear
covariance of $m_{0}(X)$ with the part of $p(X)$ not linearly
explained by $X$. With no restriction on the functional forms of
$m_{0}$ and $p$ this can be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$ with
$w(X)=p(X)-0.6$, gives ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}Y$ coefficient on $D$
$\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for
every $X$. The non-parametric partial effect
$E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but the linear projection
coefficient is $ {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ and can
reverse sign because $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\neq0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear
in $X$.

Hence without a parametric linearity assumption the linear control for
$X$ does not guarantee a positive OLS coefficient. The sign is forced
only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$ let $\tau(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$. Conditional randomisation is $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, i.e.

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,\tau(X),\qquad \tau(X)>0$,

so $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]=E[Y(1)]$, $E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(0)]$ and

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE and the sign is preserved.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is correlated with $X$ marginally. The marginal mean difference is

$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[E[Y(1)\mid X]\mid D=1]-E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0]$.

Because $P(X\mid D=1)\propto p(X)P(X)$ and $P(X\mid D=0)\propto (1-p(X))P(X)$ the two averages are over different $X$-distributions. With $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ increasing in $X$ and $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ the selection term $E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=1]-E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0]$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. The classic Simpson reversal e.g. $Y(0)=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]<E[Y\mid D=0]$ despite $\tau>0$ a.s. Hence the crude regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is not sign protected.

Case 3. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and we regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$. Put $r=D-p(X)$, $E[r\mid X]=0$. Then

$E[Y\,r\mid X]=E[Y(0)\mid X]E[r\mid X]+\tau(X)E[Dr\mid X]=\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)$.

Since $E[r\mid X]=0$, $Cov(Y,r)=E[\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)]>0$. With $Var(r)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,r)/Var(r)=E[\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]$

is a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average effects $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$. In particular the Frisch-Waugh residual of $D$ after $X$ is mean independent of $X$ conditional on $X$, and $E[Y\mid X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. Controlling for $X$ removes the composition bias that flips the sign in Case 2, so the population linear partial effect of $D$ is the average of the strictly positive conditional effects and must be $>0$.

Hence positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is included in the regression, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

6.text:
The population OLS slope is the linear projection of $Y$ on the regressor of
interest after projection on the other regressors.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and under conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$,
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Binary $D$ makes the OLS slope the mean difference, so the sign is
forced by $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
   =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, 
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ can be Simpson reversed.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken.
Frisch-Waugh gives
$\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ with
$\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$.
Write ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)=a+bX$. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\!\left[ h(X){\rm Cov}(D,\tilde D\mid X)\right]
+E\!\left[m_{0}(X)\tilde D\right]$.
Now $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-a-bX\neq0$ in general, so the second term is
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ with $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
With a non-linear propensity $p(X)$ the residual $w(X)$ is non-zero and
$m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w(X)$ to make
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ arbitrarily negative while keeping $h(X)>0$.
E.g. $X\in[0,1]$, $p(X)=X^{2}$, $h\equiv1$ and
$m_{0}(X)=-K\big(p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ gives
$\beta_{D}<0$ for $K$ large enough, even though
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Hence the non-parametric partial effect $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$
is preserved, but the linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not.  The sign of
the OLS coefficient is not guaranteed under conditional randomisation
without a linearity restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$, which is
ruled out by the “no parametric assumptions’’ requirement.

So sign preservation holds only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Only Case 1

Write $Y = Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with
$h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.
Put $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
For a binary $D$ the population OLS slope in $Y\sim1+D$ is exactly the mean
difference, so $\beta_{D}>0$ a.s.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)+h(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The two expectations are under $P(X\mid D=1)$ vs $P(X\mid D=0)$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the
selection term can dominate the positive $h$ term.  
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$ slope can be
$<0$ despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\beta_{X}X+u$ is taken.
Let $\tilde D=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of $D$. Then
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)+e$,

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]+E[h(X)E[D\mid X]
(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D)]+E[m_{0}(X)(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D)]$.

The first term is $>0$ but the last two involve the linear projection error
$E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D$. When $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ is non-linear in $X$ this
error is non-zero and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with
$m_{0}(X)$. 

Take $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$ so
$\Pi_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$ and $Res_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$. Put $h\equiv1$ and
$m_{0}(X)=-K\,Res_{p}(X)$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every
$X$, but 
$\beta_{D}= (1-K)/3$, which is $<0$ for $K>1$. With a large enough $K$ the
linear $1+D+X$ projection has a negative $D$ loading even though the
conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$ at every $X$.

Hence non-parametric conditional randomisation does not preserve the sign
in the linear projection on $1,D,X$. The sign is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.

8.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$,

$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$, $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
The population OLS coefficient in $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ is

$\beta =\frac{{\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)}{{\rm Var}(\tilde D)}
      =\frac{E[\tilde D\,m_{0}(X)]}{ {\rm Var}(\tilde D)}
       +\frac{E[\tilde D\,D\,h(X)]}{ {\rm Var}(\tilde D)} $.

Now $E[\tilde D\,D\mid X]=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\mid X]$ so that the second
term is a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$.  The first term is

$E[\tilde D\,m_{0}(X)]=E\big[\,w(X)m_{0}(X)\,\big]$,

$w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.

Hence $\beta>0$ is the sign of $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
$w(X)$ is zero iff $p(X)$ is affine in $X$, otherwise it is a non-zero
mean-zero function orthogonal to $1,X$.  With no restriction on $m_{0}$
we can make $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$,
$w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$ and $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$.  Then
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet

${\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$.

So the linear coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ can be negative even
though $E[Y\mid D=1,X]>E[Y\mid D=0,X]$ a.s.  The sign-preserving
expression $E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ holds for
the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, not for the linear residual
$\tilde D$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. Now
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$,
and with $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$
the selection term can dominate.  With $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The crude $D$ coefficient can be
negative.

Hence with the stated no-parametric restriction the sign is forced only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Only Case 1

With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s. put
$m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ and $h(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$.
Conditional randomisation is 
$E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then 
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
The simple regression is the ATE and positivity of $\tau_{i}$ forces 
$\beta_{1}>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but the selection term 
$E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when
$P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ is monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. 
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$ though $\tau>0$ a.s. The marginal 
mean difference is not sign protected.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the linear projection 
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken. 
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm proj}_{1,X}(D)$. Then 
$\beta_{D}=Cov(\tilde D,Y)/Var(\tilde D)$. Writing $Y=m_{0}(X)+D h(X)+\varepsilon$,

$Cov(\tilde D,Y)=Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))+E\big[h(X)E[\tilde D D|X]\big]$.

The second term is $>0$, the first term is $Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))$ 
and $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only linearly, not to arbitrary 
functions of $X$.  With $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$ the residual
$w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is non-zero and $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Choosing $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ with $K>0$ large makes
$Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))$ arbitrarily negative while $h(X)>0$ is kept
fixed. Then $Cov(\tilde D,Y)<0$ and $\beta_{D}<0$ even though
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

The non-parametric partial effect
$E\big[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)\big]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$
is the coefficient on the residual $D-E[D|X]$, not on the linear
residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. With no parametric restriction on
$m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$ the linear OLS coefficient need not keep
the sign of the conditional monotone effect.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS slope on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be reversed by
selection on $X$, the latter by non-linearity of $E[D|X]$ and of $m_{0}(X)$
relative to the linear span $\{1,X\}$.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., and conditional unconfoundedness $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ we have

$E[Y\mid D,X]=E[Y_{0}\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]$

with $h(X):=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.  So for every $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$ and the intercept-slope regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE. The sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D$ is in general dependent on $X$ marginally. The crude coefficient is

$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$

with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$. The first term is $>0$ but the selection term $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when $P(D=1\mid X)$ is monotone opposite to $m(X)$. The classic $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $P(D=1\mid X=0)=0.9$, $P(D=1\mid X=1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]<E[Y\mid D=0]$. So the marginal regression of $Y$ on $D$ alone is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now we condition on $X$. Write $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ and $\eta=D-p(X)$ so $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Then

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta\,m(X)]+E[\eta D h(X)]=E[\eta D h(X)]$

because $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. With $E[\eta D\mid X]=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)$,

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)h(X)\big]$

and $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]$. Hence in population

$\beta_{D}= \frac{E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)h(X)\big]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]}$

is a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average effects $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ with weights $w(X)=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))\ge0$. On the support where $0<p(X)<1$ the weight is strictly positive, so $\beta_{D}>0$.

That is the Frisch-Waugh intuition: after removing the part of $D$ that is predictable from $X$, the residual variation in $D$ is mean-independent of $X$ and $E[Y\mid D,X]$ is monotone in $D$ for every $X$. Controlling for pre-treatment income removes the composition bias that can flip the sign in Case 2 and the population partial effect of $D$ is a positive weighted average of the positive conditional gains.

The non-linear $p(X)$ constructions that are quoted as making a linear projection on $1,X,D$ negative rely on interpreting “control for $X$” as a linear projection $D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}D$ and then choosing $m(X)$ to be perfectly anti-correlated with the linear residual $p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. That is a knife-edge, essentially a fine-tuned correlation between the baseline mean function $m(X)$ and the linear approximation error of the propensity, not a generic consequence of $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau>0$. In the usual conditioning interpretation the residual is $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is by construction orthogonal to any function of $X$, and the partial coefficient is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted mean above.

Hence sign preservation holds for the unconditionally randomised comparison and for the comparison with $X$ included, but not for the unadjusted comparison under conditional randomisation.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I agree with the group on Case 1 and on the sign problem in Case 2.

Case 1: D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1). Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0 and the population OLS slope of Y on a constant and D is exactly that mean difference. Positivity is guaranteed.

Case 2: D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1) | X but D is not marginally independent of X. 
With Y=Y(0)+Dτ, τ>0 a.s.,
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[E[Y(1)|X]|D=1]-E[E[Y(0)|X]|D=0].
The two conditional expectations are taken under P(X|D=1) and P(X|D=0) which differ whenever P(D=1|X) varies with X. With Y(0)=f(X) increasing and P(D=1|X) decreasing in X the composition term E[f(X)|D=1]-E[f(X)|D=0] can outweigh the positive c=E[τ|X]>0. The X∈{0,1} example with p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 and Y0=100X, τ≡1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90. The marginal regression of Y on D alone is not sign protected. That is the classic Simpson reversal under conditional randomisation.

Case 3 is different. With D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1) | X we have
E[Y|X,D]=E[Y0|X]+D E[τ|X] ≡ m0(X)+D h(X),    h(X)=E[τ|X]>0 a.s.
Write D = E[D|X]+η with E[η|X]=0 and E[η m0(X)|X]=0, E[η h(X)|X]=h(X)E[η|X]=0 for the part in m0.
Then
Cov(Y,η)=Cov(m0(X)+D h(X),η)=E[Cov(D h(X),η|X)]=E[h(X) Cov(D,η|X)].
Because Cov(D,η|X)=Var(D|X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0 on the support,
Cov(Y,η)=E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ]>0.
Up to the usual Frisch-Waugh re-scaling the population coefficient on D in the regression of Y on 1,D,X is
β = E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] / E[ Var(D|X) ] ,
i.e. a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional mean effects h(X) with weights Var(D|X)≥0. The residual variation in D after partialling out X is mean independent of X, so any function of X, in particular m0(X), is orthogonal to the residual. The only term that remains is the positive conditional gain h(X) multiplied by the conditional variance of D.

Controlling for X therefore removes the selection term that can flip the sign in Case 2. The OLS slope is the average of E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0 over the distribution of X weighted by the conditional variance of treatment. Hence it must be >0.

The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection of Y on 1,D,X rely on confusing the population linear projection residual D-Proj_{1,X}D with the conditional expectation residual D-E[D|X]. The latter is mean independent of X and orthogonal to any function of X. Once X is partialled out in the population, the remaining variation in D is conditionally randomised and the coefficient is the positive weighted average of h(X)>0. With strictly positive individual effects, the sign is preserved in Case 1 and in Case 3, but not in the marginal regression of Case 2.

11.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with
$m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$.
For binary $D$, $\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ where
$\tilde D$ is the residual from the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$.

* Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
With a binary $D$ the regression $Y=\alpha+\beta D+u$ has
$\beta=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]>0$ in the population. Unconditional
randomisation is sign preserving.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
$h(X)>0$ but $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative
by making $p(X)=E[D|X]$ decreasing in $X$ while $m(X)$ is increasing in
$X$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The crude
intercept-slope coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ and can be $<0$.

* Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$. Put $D=a+bX+\tilde D$ with $a=E[D]$, $b={\rm Cov}(D,X)/{\rm
Var}(X)$. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[\tilde D\,m(X)\big]+E\big[\tilde D\,D\,h(X)\big]$.
With $r_{p}(X)=p(X)-a-bX$ the part of the propensity that is not linear
in $X$, $\tilde D=r_{p}(X)+\eta$ with $E[\eta|X]=0$,

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]+E\big[ h(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big]
+E[r_{p}(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

The second term is $>0$, but $E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]$ is the linear covariance
of the baseline mean function with the non-linear part of the
propensity score and can be made arbitrarily negative.  With
$X=0,1,2$, $P(X=x)=1/3$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$,
$a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=0.24-0.08K$, ${\rm Var}(\tilde D)=0.24$ and
$\beta_{D}=1-K/3<0$ for $K>3$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give
${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but the OLS residual
is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D|X]$.  Without linearity of
$m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the linear projection on $1,X$ does not
partial out $X$ non-parametrically and the sign of the population
coefficient on $D$ is not preserved.

Hence a strictly positive individual effect forces a positive
population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2
and Case 3 can both be sign reversed.

A. Only Case 1.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think E is the right characterisation.

Case 1 is uncontroversial. With unconditional randomisation
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ so $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$ and the OLS
intercept–slope regression of $Y$ on $D$ is exactly that ATE. Positivity of
$\tau_i$ for every $i$ forces the population slope to be $>0$.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson case.  Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ we have
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=E[\tau|X]>0$ for every $X$, but the marginal
comparison integrates over different $X$ distributions:
$E[Y|D=1]=E\{E[Y(1)|X]\mid D=1\}$ and $E[Y|D=0]=E\{E[Y(0)|X]\mid D=0\}$.
If $P(D=1|X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while $E[Y(0)|X]$ is increasing in $X$
the composition effect can dominate the positive gain.  The usual
$X\in\{0,1\}$ example with $P(D=1|X=0)=0.9$, $P(D=1|X=1)=0.1$ and
$Y(0)=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ despite
$\tau_i>0$ a.s.  So the crude regression of $Y$ on a constant and $D$ alone
is not sign protected under conditional randomisation.

Once $X$ is in the regression the selection bias is removed.  Write
$m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Conditional
unconfoundedness gives
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s.
Let $\eta=D-p(X)$.  Then $E[\eta|X]=0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta\{m_0(X)+D h(X)\}]
=E[\,h(X)E[D\eta|X]\,] =E[\,h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,] >0$.
With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$,
the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$ part is
$$
\beta_{D}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)}{\operatorname{Var}(\eta)}
=\frac{E[\,h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}
=\sum_{x} w(x)h(x),
$$
a convex weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average
treatment effects $h(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]$ with weights
$w(x)\propto \operatorname{Var}(D|X=x)=p(x)(1-p(x))>0$ on the support of $X$.
That is the Frisch-Waugh form of the OLS coefficient on $D$ in
$Y\sim 1+D+X$.  It is the average of positive numbers, hence $>0$.

Intuitively, after conditioning on pre-treatment income $X$ the treated
and control units are comparable within each $X$ stratum and the
conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$. Partialling out $X$, i.e.
working with the $X$-residualised variation in $D$, is therefore
positively correlated with the $X$-residualised outcome.  Controlling for
$X$ removes the composition bias that can flip the sign in Case 2 and
recovers the sign of the treatment effect.

So we have a guaranteed positive population slope for the unconditionally
randomised regression, and also for the regression that conditions on $X$,
but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That
is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

10.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s.,

$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and
$h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  For binary $D$
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
The intercept–slope OLS is the mean difference and is strictly
positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.  Then
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
        =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]\neq E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$
in general because $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ can be monotone opposite to
$m_{0}(X)$.  E.g. $Y_{0}=100X,\;\tau\equiv1,\;p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<E[Y\mid D=0]=90$. The marginal mean difference
and hence the OLS slope of $Y$ on $1,D$ can be negative.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear
projection on $1,D,X$,

$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)$,
$\tilde D=D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
with $a=E[D]-bE[X]$, $b=\operatorname{Cov}(D,X)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

Writing $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]
      +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)h(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term is $>0$, the second is the linear residual covariance
of $E[Y\mid X]$ with the residualised propensity $w(X)$.
With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}$ or $p$, $w(X)$ can be made
non-zero, e.g. $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen
anti-correlated with $w(X)$.  Then
$\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative and
dominate $E[h\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]$.
For instance $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8,\;p(1)=0.2$,
$m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$, $h\equiv1$, gives $\beta_{D}\propto 1-K<0$ for
$K>1$ although $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Hence the linear OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced to be $>0$ only under
unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can both change sign under
the maintained positivity of $\tau_{i}>0$ and no further parametric
restriction.

A. Only Case 1.

2.text:
With the potential outcomes write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and under
conditional randomisation

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$$
a.s.  Let $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Case 1  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then
$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$$
and with a binary $D$ the population regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the mean
difference.  Positivity of $\tau_{i}$ for every $i$ therefore forces
$\beta_{1}>0$ in the population.

Case 2  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.  Now
$$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E\big[m(X)+h(X)\mid D=1\big]-E\big[m(X)\mid D=0\big]
 =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0],$$
the last term being the selection bias $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can
dominate the positive $E[h(X)\mid D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.  Hence the simple OLS slope
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]$ can be $<0$ despite $\tau_{i}>0$
a.s.

Case 3  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$.  Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$,
$E[\tilde D]=E[\tilde D X]=0$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$.  Then
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[m(X)\tilde D\big]+E\big[h(X)D\tilde D\big]
 =E\big[r(X)m(X)\big]+E\big[r(X)p(X)h(X)\big]+E\big[h(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big].
$$
With $E[\tilde D\mid X]=r(X)$ the term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linearly
partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$.  Because no parametric form for
$m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is imposed $r(X)$ can be made non-zero and
oppositely correlated with $m(X)$.  Writing
$D=p(X)+e$, $E[e\mid X]=0$, $\tilde D=r(X)+e$,
$$
\beta_{D}=\frac{E[r(X)\{m(X)+p(X)h(X)\}]+E[h(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]}
               {E[r(X)^{2}]+E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]},
$$
so the sign is the sign of $E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]$ plus a positive
term.  Choosing $m(X)=-K\,r(X)$ with $K>0$ large makes the numerator
arbitrarily negative while keeping $h(X)>0$ and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.  The classic example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $m(X)=-K r(X)$, $h\equiv1$, gives
$\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.  Hence the linear projection coefficient on $D$
in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not sign protected; the non-parametric partial effect
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ is the coefficient
on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.

Thus a strictly positive population OLS slope is forced by $\tau_{i}>0$
a.s. only under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can be sign
reversed by a non-linear $p(X)$ and a suitably chosen $m(X)$.  This is
option A, Only Case 1.

public_text.4:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s.,

$$
E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad 
E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0 .
$$

* Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$
and for a binary $D$ the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly this mean
difference. Unconditional randomisation therefore preserves the sign.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$
The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be
arbitrarily negative when $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while
$m_{0}(X)$ is increasing.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  
Hence the crude OLS $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ is not sign-preserved.

* Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$.
Write $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ with
$w(X)=E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX$.
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]
+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)] .
$$
The first term is $>0$. The term $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ is the linear
covariance of $m_{0}(X)$ with the part of $p(X)$ not linearly
explained by $X$. With no restriction on the functional forms of
$m_{0}$ and $p$ this can be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$ with
$w(X)=p(X)-0.6$, gives ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}Y$ coefficient on $D$
$\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for
every $X$. The non-parametric partial effect
$E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but the linear projection
coefficient is $ {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ and can
reverse sign because $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\neq0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear
in $X$.

Hence without a parametric linearity assumption the linear control for
$X$ does not guarantee a positive OLS coefficient. The sign is forced
only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1
public_text.1:
With potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$ let $\tau(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$. Conditional randomisation is $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, i.e.

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,\tau(X),\qquad \tau(X)>0$,

so $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]=E[Y(1)]$, $E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(0)]$ and

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE and the sign is preserved.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is correlated with $X$ marginally. The marginal mean difference is

$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[E[Y(1)\mid X]\mid D=1]-E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0]$.

Because $P(X\mid D=1)\propto p(X)P(X)$ and $P(X\mid D=0)\propto (1-p(X))P(X)$ the two averages are over different $X$-distributions. With $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ increasing in $X$ and $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ the selection term $E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=1]-E[E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0]$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. The classic Simpson reversal e.g. $Y(0)=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]<E[Y\mid D=0]$ despite $\tau>0$ a.s. Hence the crude regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is not sign protected.

Case 3. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and we regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$. Put $r=D-p(X)$, $E[r\mid X]=0$. Then

$E[Y\,r\mid X]=E[Y(0)\mid X]E[r\mid X]+\tau(X)E[Dr\mid X]=\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)$.

Since $E[r\mid X]=0$, $Cov(Y,r)=E[\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)]>0$. With $Var(r)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,r)/Var(r)=E[\tau(X)Var(D\mid X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]$

is a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average effects $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$. In particular the Frisch-Waugh residual of $D$ after $X$ is mean independent of $X$ conditional on $X$, and $E[Y\mid X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. Controlling for $X$ removes the composition bias that flips the sign in Case 2, so the population linear partial effect of $D$ is the average of the strictly positive conditional effects and must be $>0$.

Hence positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is included in the regression, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.
public_text.6:
The population OLS slope is the linear projection of $Y$ on the regressor of
interest after projection on the other regressors.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and under conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$,
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Binary $D$ makes the OLS slope the mean difference, so the sign is
forced by $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
   =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, 
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ can be Simpson reversed.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken.
Frisch-Waugh gives
$\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ with
$\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$.
Write ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)=a+bX$. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\!\left[ h(X){\rm Cov}(D,\tilde D\mid X)\right]
+E\!\left[m_{0}(X)\tilde D\right]$.
Now $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-a-bX\neq0$ in general, so the second term is
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ with $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
With a non-linear propensity $p(X)$ the residual $w(X)$ is non-zero and
$m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w(X)$ to make
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ arbitrarily negative while keeping $h(X)>0$.
E.g. $X\in[0,1]$, $p(X)=X^{2}$, $h\equiv1$ and
$m_{0}(X)=-K\big(p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ gives
$\beta_{D}<0$ for $K$ large enough, even though
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Hence the non-parametric partial effect $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$
is preserved, but the linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not.  The sign of
the OLS coefficient is not guaranteed under conditional randomisation
without a linearity restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$, which is
ruled out by the “no parametric assumptions’’ requirement.

So sign preservation holds only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

A. Only Case 1

Write $Y = Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with
$h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.
Put $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
For a binary $D$ the population OLS slope in $Y\sim1+D$ is exactly the mean
difference, so $\beta_{D}>0$ a.s.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)+h(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The two expectations are under $P(X\mid D=1)$ vs $P(X\mid D=0)$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the
selection term can dominate the positive $h$ term.  
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$ slope can be
$<0$ despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\beta_{X}X+u$ is taken.
Let $\tilde D=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of $D$. Then
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)+e$,

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]+E[h(X)E[D\mid X]
(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D)]+E[m_{0}(X)(E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D)]$.

The first term is $>0$ but the last two involve the linear projection error
$E[D\mid X]-\Pi_{1,X}D$. When $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ is non-linear in $X$ this
error is non-zero and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with
$m_{0}(X)$. 

Take $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$ so
$\Pi_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$ and $Res_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$. Put $h\equiv1$ and
$m_{0}(X)=-K\,Res_{p}(X)$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every
$X$, but 
$\beta_{D}= (1-K)/3$, which is $<0$ for $K>1$. With a large enough $K$ the
linear $1+D+X$ projection has a negative $D$ loading even though the
conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$ at every $X$.

Hence non-parametric conditional randomisation does not preserve the sign
in the linear projection on $1,D,X$. The sign is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.
public_text.8:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$,

$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$, $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
The population OLS coefficient in $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ is

$\beta =\frac{{\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)}{{\rm Var}(\tilde D)}
      =\frac{E[\tilde D\,m_{0}(X)]}{ {\rm Var}(\tilde D)}
       +\frac{E[\tilde D\,D\,h(X)]}{ {\rm Var}(\tilde D)} $.

Now $E[\tilde D\,D\mid X]=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\mid X]$ so that the second
term is a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$.  The first term is

$E[\tilde D\,m_{0}(X)]=E\big[\,w(X)m_{0}(X)\,\big]$,

$w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.

Hence $\beta>0$ is the sign of $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
$w(X)$ is zero iff $p(X)$ is affine in $X$, otherwise it is a non-zero
mean-zero function orthogonal to $1,X$.  With no restriction on $m_{0}$
we can make $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$,
$w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$ and $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$.  Then
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet

${\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$.

So the linear coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ can be negative even
though $E[Y\mid D=1,X]>E[Y\mid D=0,X]$ a.s.  The sign-preserving
expression $E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ holds for
the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, not for the linear residual
$\tilde D$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. Now
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$,
and with $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$
the selection term can dominate.  With $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The crude $D$ coefficient can be
negative.

Hence with the stated no-parametric restriction the sign is forced only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

A. Only Case 1

With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s. put
$m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ and $h(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$.
Conditional randomisation is 
$E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then 
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
The simple regression is the ATE and positivity of $\tau_{i}$ forces 
$\beta_{1}>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but the selection term 
$E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when
$P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ is monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. 
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$ though $\tau>0$ a.s. The marginal 
mean difference is not sign protected.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the linear projection 
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken. 
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm proj}_{1,X}(D)$. Then 
$\beta_{D}=Cov(\tilde D,Y)/Var(\tilde D)$. Writing $Y=m_{0}(X)+D h(X)+\varepsilon$,

$Cov(\tilde D,Y)=Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))+E\big[h(X)E[\tilde D D|X]\big]$.

The second term is $>0$, the first term is $Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))$ 
and $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only linearly, not to arbitrary 
functions of $X$.  With $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$ the residual
$w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is non-zero and $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Choosing $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ with $K>0$ large makes
$Cov(\tilde D,m_{0}(X))$ arbitrarily negative while $h(X)>0$ is kept
fixed. Then $Cov(\tilde D,Y)<0$ and $\beta_{D}<0$ even though
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

The non-parametric partial effect
$E\big[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)\big]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$
is the coefficient on the residual $D-E[D|X]$, not on the linear
residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. With no parametric restriction on
$m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$ the linear OLS coefficient need not keep
the sign of the conditional monotone effect.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS slope on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be reversed by
selection on $X$, the latter by non-linearity of $E[D|X]$ and of $m_{0}(X)$
relative to the linear span $\{1,X\}$.
public_text.5:
E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., and conditional unconfoundedness $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ we have

$E[Y\mid D,X]=E[Y_{0}\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]$

with $h(X):=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.  So for every $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$ and the intercept-slope regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE. The sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D$ is in general dependent on $X$ marginally. The crude coefficient is

$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$

with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$. The first term is $>0$ but the selection term $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ can be arbitrarily negative when $P(D=1\mid X)$ is monotone opposite to $m(X)$. The classic $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $P(D=1\mid X=0)=0.9$, $P(D=1\mid X=1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]<E[Y\mid D=0]$. So the marginal regression of $Y$ on $D$ alone is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now we condition on $X$. Write $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ and $\eta=D-p(X)$ so $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Then

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta\,m(X)]+E[\eta D h(X)]=E[\eta D h(X)]$

because $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. With $E[\eta D\mid X]=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)$,

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)h(X)\big]$

and $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]$. Hence in population

$\beta_{D}= \frac{E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)h(X)\big]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]}$

is a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average effects $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ with weights $w(X)=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))\ge0$. On the support where $0<p(X)<1$ the weight is strictly positive, so $\beta_{D}>0$.

That is the Frisch-Waugh intuition: after removing the part of $D$ that is predictable from $X$, the residual variation in $D$ is mean-independent of $X$ and $E[Y\mid D,X]$ is monotone in $D$ for every $X$. Controlling for pre-treatment income removes the composition bias that can flip the sign in Case 2 and the population partial effect of $D$ is a positive weighted average of the positive conditional gains.

The non-linear $p(X)$ constructions that are quoted as making a linear projection on $1,X,D$ negative rely on interpreting “control for $X$” as a linear projection $D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}D$ and then choosing $m(X)$ to be perfectly anti-correlated with the linear residual $p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. That is a knife-edge, essentially a fine-tuned correlation between the baseline mean function $m(X)$ and the linear approximation error of the propensity, not a generic consequence of $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau>0$. In the usual conditioning interpretation the residual is $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is by construction orthogonal to any function of $X$, and the partial coefficient is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted mean above.

Hence sign preservation holds for the unconditionally randomised comparison and for the comparison with $X$ included, but not for the unadjusted comparison under conditional randomisation.
public_text.7:
E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I agree with the group on Case 1 and on the sign problem in Case 2.

Case 1: D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1). Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0 and the population OLS slope of Y on a constant and D is exactly that mean difference. Positivity is guaranteed.

Case 2: D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1) | X but D is not marginally independent of X. 
With Y=Y(0)+Dτ, τ>0 a.s.,
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[E[Y(1)|X]|D=1]-E[E[Y(0)|X]|D=0].
The two conditional expectations are taken under P(X|D=1) and P(X|D=0) which differ whenever P(D=1|X) varies with X. With Y(0)=f(X) increasing and P(D=1|X) decreasing in X the composition term E[f(X)|D=1]-E[f(X)|D=0] can outweigh the positive c=E[τ|X]>0. The X∈{0,1} example with p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 and Y0=100X, τ≡1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90. The marginal regression of Y on D alone is not sign protected. That is the classic Simpson reversal under conditional randomisation.

Case 3 is different. With D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1) | X we have
E[Y|X,D]=E[Y0|X]+D E[τ|X] ≡ m0(X)+D h(X),    h(X)=E[τ|X]>0 a.s.
Write D = E[D|X]+η with E[η|X]=0 and E[η m0(X)|X]=0, E[η h(X)|X]=h(X)E[η|X]=0 for the part in m0.
Then
Cov(Y,η)=Cov(m0(X)+D h(X),η)=E[Cov(D h(X),η|X)]=E[h(X) Cov(D,η|X)].
Because Cov(D,η|X)=Var(D|X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0 on the support,
Cov(Y,η)=E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ]>0.
Up to the usual Frisch-Waugh re-scaling the population coefficient on D in the regression of Y on 1,D,X is
β = E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] / E[ Var(D|X) ] ,
i.e. a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional mean effects h(X) with weights Var(D|X)≥0. The residual variation in D after partialling out X is mean independent of X, so any function of X, in particular m0(X), is orthogonal to the residual. The only term that remains is the positive conditional gain h(X) multiplied by the conditional variance of D.

Controlling for X therefore removes the selection term that can flip the sign in Case 2. The OLS slope is the average of E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0 over the distribution of X weighted by the conditional variance of treatment. Hence it must be >0.

The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection of Y on 1,D,X rely on confusing the population linear projection residual D-Proj_{1,X}D with the conditional expectation residual D-E[D|X]. The latter is mean independent of X and orthogonal to any function of X. Once X is partialled out in the population, the remaining variation in D is conditionally randomised and the coefficient is the positive weighted average of h(X)>0. With strictly positive individual effects, the sign is preserved in Case 1 and in Case 3, but not in the marginal regression of Case 2.
