The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with
$m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$.
For binary $D$, $\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ where
$\tilde D$ is the residual from the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$.

* Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
With a binary $D$ the regression $Y=\alpha+\beta D+u$ has
$\beta=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]>0$ in the population. Unconditional
randomisation is sign preserving.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
$h(X)>0$ but $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative
by making $p(X)=E[D|X]$ decreasing in $X$ while $m(X)$ is increasing in
$X$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The crude
intercept-slope coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ and can be $<0$.

* Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$. Put $D=a+bX+\tilde D$ with $a=E[D]$, $b={\rm Cov}(D,X)/{\rm
Var}(X)$. Then
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[\tilde D\,m(X)\big]+E\big[\tilde D\,D\,h(X)\big]$.
With $r_{p}(X)=p(X)-a-bX$ the part of the propensity that is not linear
in $X$, $\tilde D=r_{p}(X)+\eta$ with $E[\eta|X]=0$,

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]+E\big[ h(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big]
+E[r_{p}(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

The second term is $>0$, but $E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]$ is the linear covariance
of the baseline mean function with the non-linear part of the
propensity score and can be made arbitrarily negative.  With
$X=0,1,2$, $P(X=x)=1/3$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$,
$a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$ and
$m(X)=-K\,r_{p}(X)$, $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D$,

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=0.24-0.08K$, ${\rm Var}(\tilde D)=0.24$ and
$\beta_{D}=1-K/3<0$ for $K>3$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give
${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but the OLS residual
is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D|X]$.  Without linearity of
$m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the linear projection on $1,X$ does not
partial out $X$ non-parametrically and the sign of the population
coefficient on $D$ is not preserved.

Hence a strictly positive individual effect forces a positive
population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2
and Case 3 can both be sign reversed.

A. Only Case 1.
public_text.12:
I think E is the right characterisation.

Case 1 is uncontroversial. With unconditional randomisation
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ so $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$ and the OLS
intercept–slope regression of $Y$ on $D$ is exactly that ATE. Positivity of
$\tau_i$ for every $i$ forces the population slope to be $>0$.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson case.  Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ we have
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=E[\tau|X]>0$ for every $X$, but the marginal
comparison integrates over different $X$ distributions:
$E[Y|D=1]=E\{E[Y(1)|X]\mid D=1\}$ and $E[Y|D=0]=E\{E[Y(0)|X]\mid D=0\}$.
If $P(D=1|X)$ is decreasing in $X$ while $E[Y(0)|X]$ is increasing in $X$
the composition effect can dominate the positive gain.  The usual
$X\in\{0,1\}$ example with $P(D=1|X=0)=0.9$, $P(D=1|X=1)=0.1$ and
$Y(0)=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ despite
$\tau_i>0$ a.s.  So the crude regression of $Y$ on a constant and $D$ alone
is not sign protected under conditional randomisation.

Once $X$ is in the regression the selection bias is removed.  Write
$m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Conditional
unconfoundedness gives
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s.
Let $\eta=D-p(X)$.  Then $E[\eta|X]=0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta\{m_0(X)+D h(X)\}]
=E[\,h(X)E[D\eta|X]\,] =E[\,h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,] >0$.
With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$,
the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$ part is
$$
\beta_{D}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)}{\operatorname{Var}(\eta)}
=\frac{E[\,h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}
=\sum_{x} w(x)h(x),
$$
a convex weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average
treatment effects $h(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]$ with weights
$w(x)\propto \operatorname{Var}(D|X=x)=p(x)(1-p(x))>0$ on the support of $X$.
That is the Frisch-Waugh form of the OLS coefficient on $D$ in
$Y\sim 1+D+X$.  It is the average of positive numbers, hence $>0$.

Intuitively, after conditioning on pre-treatment income $X$ the treated
and control units are comparable within each $X$ stratum and the
conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$. Partialling out $X$, i.e.
working with the $X$-residualised variation in $D$, is therefore
positively correlated with the $X$-residualised outcome.  Controlling for
$X$ removes the composition bias that can flip the sign in Case 2 and
recovers the sign of the treatment effect.

So we have a guaranteed positive population slope for the unconditionally
randomised regression, and also for the regression that conditions on $X$,
but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That
is Only Case 1 and Case 3.
public_text.10:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s.,

$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and
$h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ under $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  For binary $D$
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
The intercept–slope OLS is the mean difference and is strictly
positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.  Then
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
        =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]\neq E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$
in general because $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ can be monotone opposite to
$m_{0}(X)$.  E.g. $Y_{0}=100X,\;\tau\equiv1,\;p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<E[Y\mid D=0]=90$. The marginal mean difference
and hence the OLS slope of $Y$ on $1,D$ can be negative.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear
projection on $1,D,X$,

$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)$,
$\tilde D=D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
with $a=E[D]-bE[X]$, $b=\operatorname{Cov}(D,X)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

Writing $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]
      +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)h(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term is $>0$, the second is the linear residual covariance
of $E[Y\mid X]$ with the residualised propensity $w(X)$.
With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}$ or $p$, $w(X)$ can be made
non-zero, e.g. $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen
anti-correlated with $w(X)$.  Then
$\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative and
dominate $E[h\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)]$.
For instance $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8,\;p(1)=0.2$,
$m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$, $h\equiv1$, gives $\beta_{D}\propto 1-K<0$ for
$K>1$ although $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Hence the linear OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced to be $>0$ only under
unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can both change sign under
the maintained positivity of $\tau_{i}>0$ and no further parametric
restriction.

A. Only Case 1.
public_text.2:
With the potential outcomes write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and under
conditional randomisation

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$$
a.s.  Let $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

Case 1  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then
$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$$
and with a binary $D$ the population regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the mean
difference.  Positivity of $\tau_{i}$ for every $i$ therefore forces
$\beta_{1}>0$ in the population.

Case 2  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.  Now
$$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E\big[m(X)+h(X)\mid D=1\big]-E\big[m(X)\mid D=0\big]
 =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0],$$
the last term being the selection bias $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can
dominate the positive $E[h(X)\mid D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.  Hence the simple OLS slope
$\beta_{D}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]$ can be $<0$ despite $\tau_{i}>0$
a.s.

Case 3  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$.  Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$,
$E[\tilde D]=E[\tilde D X]=0$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$.  Then
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[m(X)\tilde D\big]+E\big[h(X)D\tilde D\big]
 =E\big[r(X)m(X)\big]+E\big[r(X)p(X)h(X)\big]+E\big[h(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big].
$$
With $E[\tilde D\mid X]=r(X)$ the term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linearly
partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$.  Because no parametric form for
$m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is imposed $r(X)$ can be made non-zero and
oppositely correlated with $m(X)$.  Writing
$D=p(X)+e$, $E[e\mid X]=0$, $\tilde D=r(X)+e$,
$$
\beta_{D}=\frac{E[r(X)\{m(X)+p(X)h(X)\}]+E[h(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]}
               {E[r(X)^{2}]+E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]},
$$
so the sign is the sign of $E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]$ plus a positive
term.  Choosing $m(X)=-K\,r(X)$ with $K>0$ large makes the numerator
arbitrarily negative while keeping $h(X)>0$ and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.  The classic example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $m(X)=-K r(X)$, $h\equiv1$, gives
$\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.  Hence the linear projection coefficient on $D$
in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not sign protected; the non-parametric partial effect
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ is the coefficient
on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.

Thus a strictly positive population OLS slope is forced by $\tau_{i}>0$
a.s. only under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can be sign
reversed by a non-linear $p(X)$ and a suitably chosen $m(X)$.  This is
option A, Only Case 1.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., potential outcomes. Conditional randomisation $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ gives $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ and for binary $D$ the population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Positivity is guaranteed. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. The marginal OLS coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$. The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, the marginal difference can be negative despite $h(X)>0$ a.s. Classic example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Unanimous.

Case 3. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$. The population coefficient is $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, i.e. $D-a-bX$. Write $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

The first term $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]>0$. The second term is the linear covariance of the baseline mean $m_{0}(X)$ with the non-linear part of the propensity $w(X)$. With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$, $w(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w(X)$ to make $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative. E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $a=0.6,b=0$, $w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The strictly positive expression $E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the coefficient on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, which is mean independent of any function of $X$. It is not the coefficient on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ unless $E[D|X]$ is affine in $X$ and/or $m_{0}$ and $h$ are affine. The colleagues arguing for E Only Case1 and Case3 e.g. 1,12,6,7,9 are effectively using $E[\tilde D|X]=0$, i.e. treating the OLS control for $X$ as non-parametric residualisation. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 point out the $w(X)$ term and give explicit counterexamples showing the linear projection can reverse sign.

Under the instruction “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the linear control is only linear in $X$, so the sign is not guaranteed. The only case forced positive is unconditional randomisation.

Current belief: positivity guaranteed only in Case 1. Case 2 fails by marginal selection on $X$, Case 3 fails by linear approximation error when $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ are non-linear in $X$. Unresolved nuance is the distinction between the non-parametric partial effect $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ and the linear OLS coefficient, which is what the question asks for.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The maintained model is $Y = Y_0 + D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., so under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $\beta_D=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ for binary $D$. Sign is forced.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Agreed all sides: sign not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. 
$\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Write $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[w(X)m_0(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w m_0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing $m_0$ anti-correlated with the linear residual $w$. With $p$ non-linear in $X$, $w\neq0$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0=-K w$, gives $\beta_D\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$.

The sign-preserving expression $\beta=E[Var(D|X)h(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for non-parametric control of $X$, not for the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ $m_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ can be non-linear, so the linear projection error can reverse sign.

Hence the $E$-camp 1+3 claim requires interpreting “control for $X$’’ as non-parametric partialling out. With the literal linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ the linear approximation error breaks sign preservation.

Current best reading: sign guaranteed only for unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can both be reversed. That is option A. Only Case 1. The persistent disagreement is between those who treat $X$ control as $D-E[D|X]$ vs those who keep the linear projection $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$.
Binary $D$, OLS is the linear projection.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ unconditionally.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$, marginal regression $Y\sim1+D$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The $X$ distributions under $D=1$ and $D=0$ differ when $p(X)$ is non-constant. With $m_{0}$ increasing and $p$ decreasing the selection term can dominate the positive $h$ term.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.
Sign not guaranteed.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$, linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$.
The population coefficient is $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$.
Write $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but the last two involve the linear projection error of the propensity.
If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w(X)\neq0$.
Choosing $m_{0}(X)$ anti-correlated with $w(X)$ makes $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ but $\beta_{D}\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$.
The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give $\beta^{np}=E[h Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$, a weighted average of the strictly positive conditional effects. The OLS residual is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D|X]$, so without linearity of $m_{0}$ and $p$ the sign is not preserved.

Hence under the stated no-parametric restriction the sign is forced only by unconditional randomisation. Colleagues claiming positivity in Case 3 rely on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ or implicitly assume $p(X)$ affine in $X$ and $E[Y|X]$ affine in $X$, i.e. a parametric linearity that is not allowed. The split in the room is exactly this confusion between linear projection and non-parametric partialling out of $X$.

Current belief: positivity guaranteed only in Case 1, i.e. option A. Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed by a suitable non-linear $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set-up is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$. For binary $D$ the population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly the mean difference, so the $D$ coefficient is strictly positive. Uncontroversial.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate the positive $h$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$ regression can be negative. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 agree; colleagues 1,12,5,7 claim positivity is preserved, which conflates conditional positivity with marginal positivity.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[r]=E[rX]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]$.
The last term $E[h{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial covariance.
The first term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linear partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$. With no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $r(X)$ can be non-zero when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $r(X)$ to make the covariance arbitrarily negative.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m(X)=-K\,r(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, but ${\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$. The same construction with $p(X)=X^2$ and $m(X)=-K\big(p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ yields negative OLS coefficient while the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Hence the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives
$\beta^{np}=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the argument used by colleagues 1,12,5,6,7,9 for option E. It is correct for the non-parametric partial effect but not for the linear projection $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ actually estimated by $Y\sim1+D+X$. The sign reversal requires only non-linearity of $p(X)$ in $X$, which is allowed under “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”.

Thus positivity of $\tau_i>0$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed. Current belief: Only Case 1 must be positive, option A. The disagreement in the round is exactly the confusion between $D-E[D|X]$ orthogonality to any function of $X$ and $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ orthogonality only to $1,X$.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core object is the population OLS coefficient for a binary D with
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional randomisation
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$
a.s., $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Binary $D$ gives $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign preserving.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. 
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the marginal
mean difference can be negative despite $h(X)>0$ a.s.  Classic Simpson
example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  Sign not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and OLS of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. The population
coefficient is $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with
$\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The last term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w m_{0}]$ is the linear covariance
of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity.
If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w(X)\neq0$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen
anti-correlated with $w(X)$.  E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$,
$a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives
$\beta_{D}\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, i.e. a $Var(D|X)$-weighted average
of the positive $h(X)$.  That is the argument used by the colleagues who
claim Case 3 is sign preserved.  It is the coefficient on the
non-parametric residual, not on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
With the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ the
linear projection does not remove arbitrary functions of $X$ and the sign
can flip.

Hence the only situation forced by $\tau_i>0$ a.s. to have a strictly
positive population OLS slope is unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and
3 can both be reversed by selection on $X$, Case 3 by non-linearity of
$p(X)$ and an opposite correlation of $m_{0}(X)$ with the linear projection
error. Current best belief is A. Only Case 1.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$. The marginal coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing in $X$ the composition bias dominates the positive $h$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$. All colleagues agree sign is not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear projection on $1,D,X$. With Frisch-Waugh $\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$, $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $a=E[D]-bE[X]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$.

Write $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)+w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$. The $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ term is $Cov\big(m_0(X),\,p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ and can be made arbitrarily negative when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. With no parametric restriction on $m_0$ and $p$ the linear residual is not $D-E[D|X]$, only $D-Proj_{1,X}D$, so it remains correlated with functions of $X$.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $Proj_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0(X)=-K w(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$.
The non-parametric partial effect $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ is the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-Proj_{1,X}D$. Under strict OLS linearity the sign is not forced.

Colleagues 1,12,5,6,7 argue for positivity in Case 3 by treating the residual as $D-E[D|X]$ and obtaining $\beta_D=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]$, a weighted average of $h(X)>0$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8,9 give the linear-projection counter-examples above.

Given the instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the linear projection on $1,X$ does not guarantee orthogonality to arbitrary $m_0(X)$. Hence the only sign-forced population OLS coefficient is the unconditionally randomised mean difference.

Current belief: positivity is forced only in Case 1, i.e. A. Only Case 1. Case 2 can be negative by selection on $X$, Case 3 can be negative by non-linear $p(X)$ and anti-correlated $m_0(X)$ with the linear projection error.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The maintained potential-outcome model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. For binary $D$ $\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign preserving.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ the crude mean difference can be negative e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the $Y\sim1+D$ slope is not guaranteed positive.

Case 3: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear projection on $1,D,X$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
$a=E[D]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$.  Write $r_{p}(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $w(X)=r_{p}(X)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]+E[r_{p}(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The second term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$. The first term $E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]$ is the linear covariance of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity. With no parametric restriction on $m$ and $p$ this can be made arbitrarily negative.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m(X)=-K\,r_{p}(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=0.24-0.08K$, $Var(\tilde D)=0.24$, $\beta_{D}=1-K/3<0$ for $K>3$. The sign can be reversed by choosing $m$ anti-correlated with $r_{p}$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and $\beta^{*}=E[hVar]/E[Var]>0$, a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the sign-preserving “partial out $X$” result that several colleagues cite for Case 3. It is the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. The common mistake in the deliberation is conflating the linear projection with the non-parametric partialling out.

Hence under the stated no-parametric restriction positivity of $\tau_i$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can both be signed reversed by non-linear $p(X)$ and a suitably chosen $m(X)$. Current belief remains Only Case 1, i.e. answer A. Disagreement persists with colleagues 1,5,6,7,12 who claim Case 3 is guaranteed, interpreting the regression as non-parametric control for $X$.

reflection_text.4:
The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., potential outcomes. Conditional randomisation $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ gives $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ and for binary $D$ the population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Positivity is guaranteed. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. The marginal OLS coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$. The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, the marginal difference can be negative despite $h(X)>0$ a.s. Classic example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Unanimous.

Case 3. $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$. The population coefficient is $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, i.e. $D-a-bX$. Write $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

The first term $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]>0$. The second term is the linear covariance of the baseline mean $m_{0}(X)$ with the non-linear part of the propensity $w(X)$. With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$, $w(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w(X)$ to make $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative. E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $a=0.6,b=0$, $w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $\beta_{D}=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The strictly positive expression $E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the coefficient on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, which is mean independent of any function of $X$. It is not the coefficient on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ unless $E[D|X]$ is affine in $X$ and/or $m_{0}$ and $h$ are affine. The colleagues arguing for E Only Case1 and Case3 e.g. 1,12,6,7,9 are effectively using $E[\tilde D|X]=0$, i.e. treating the OLS control for $X$ as non-parametric residualisation. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 point out the $w(X)$ term and give explicit counterexamples showing the linear projection can reverse sign.

Under the instruction “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the linear control is only linear in $X$, so the sign is not guaranteed. The only case forced positive is unconditional randomisation.

Current belief: positivity guaranteed only in Case 1. Case 2 fails by marginal selection on $X$, Case 3 fails by linear approximation error when $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ are non-linear in $X$. Unresolved nuance is the distinction between the non-parametric partial effect $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)h(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ and the linear OLS coefficient, which is what the question asks for.
reflection_text.8:
The maintained model is $Y = Y_0 + D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., so under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $\beta_D=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ for binary $D$. Sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. Marginal mean difference is $E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, selection dominates. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Agreed all sides: sign not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. 
$\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Write $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[w(X)m_0(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w m_0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing $m_0$ anti-correlated with the linear residual $w$. With $p$ non-linear in $X$, $w\neq0$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p=(0.8,0.2,0.8)$, $w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0=-K w$, gives $\beta_D\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$.

The sign-preserving expression $\beta=E[Var(D|X)h(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for non-parametric control of $X$, not for the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ $m_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ can be non-linear, so the linear projection error can reverse sign.

Hence the $E$-camp 1+3 claim requires interpreting “control for $X$’’ as non-parametric partialling out. With the literal linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ the linear approximation error breaks sign preservation.

Current best reading: sign guaranteed only for unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can both be reversed. That is option A. Only Case 1. The persistent disagreement is between those who treat $X$ control as $D-E[D|X]$ vs those who keep the linear projection $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.

The set-up is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

The selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate the positive $h$ term. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[r]=E[rX]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]$.
The last term $E[h{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial covariance.
The first term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linear partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$. With no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $r(X)$ can be non-zero when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $r(X)$ to make the covariance arbitrarily negative.

Hence the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives
$\beta^{np}=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the argument used by colleagues 1,12,5,6,7,9 for option E. The sign reversal requires only non-linearity of $p(X)$ in $X$, which is allowed under “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”.

=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign preserving.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. 
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the marginal
mean difference can be negative despite $h(X)>0$ a.s.  Classic Simpson
example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  Sign not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and OLS of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. The population
coefficient is $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with
$\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The last term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w m_{0}]$ is the linear covariance
of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity.
If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w(X)\neq0$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen
anti-correlated with $w(X)$.  E.g. $X=0,1,2$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$,
$a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives
$\beta_{D}\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, i.e. a $Var(D|X)$-weighted average
of the positive $h(X)$.  That is the argument used by the colleagues who
claim Case 3 is sign preserved.  It is the coefficient on the
non-parametric residual, not on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
With the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ the
linear projection does not remove arbitrary functions of $X$ and the sign
can flip.

Hence the only situation forced by $\tau_i>0$ a.s. to have a strictly
positive population OLS slope is unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and
3 can both be reversed by selection on $X$, Case 3 by non-linearity of
$p(X)$ and an opposite correlation of $m_{0}(X)$ with the linear projection
error. Current best belief is A. Only Case 1.

reflection_text.10:
The potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$. The marginal coefficient is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing in $X$ the composition bias dominates the positive $h$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$. All colleagues agree sign is not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear projection on $1,D,X$. With Frisch-Waugh $\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$, $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $a=E[D]-bE[X]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$.

Write $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)+w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$. The $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ term is $Cov\big(m_0(X),\,p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ and can be made arbitrarily negative when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. With no parametric restriction on $m_0$ and $p$ the linear residual is not $D-E[D|X]$, only $D-Proj_{1,X}D$, so it remains correlated with functions of $X$.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $Proj_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0(X)=-K w(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)=(1-K)/3<0$ for $K>1$.
The non-parametric partial effect $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ is the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-Proj_{1,X}D$. Under strict OLS linearity the sign is not forced.

Colleagues 1,12,5,6,7 argue for positivity in Case 3 by treating the residual as $D-E[D|X]$ and obtaining $\beta_D=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]$, a weighted average of $h(X)>0$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8,9 give the linear-projection counter-examples above.

Given the instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the linear projection on $1,X$ does not guarantee orthogonality to arbitrary $m_0(X)$. Hence the only sign-forced population OLS coefficient is the unconditionally randomised mean difference.

Current belief: positivity is forced only in Case 1, i.e. A. Only Case 1. Case 2 can be negative by selection on $X$, Case 3 can be negative by non-linear $p(X)$ and anti-correlated $m_0(X)$ with the linear projection error.
reflection_text.6:
Maintained structure is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+Dh(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. 
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$ for binary $D$.
Unconditional randomisation guarantees a positive population OLS slope. No disagreement.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term can dominate. Example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_0(X)=100X$, $h\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal regression $Y\sim1+D$ can be negative despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s. Agreed by all.

Case 3: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_D D+\gamma X+u$.
Frisch-Waugh: $\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$.
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX=:w(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[w(X)m_0(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The term $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect, but the linear residual is not $D-E[D|X]$. When $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w(X)\neq0$ and $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is unrestricted. Choosing $m_0(X)$ anti-correlated with $w(X)$ makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$. Explicit example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $\beta_D\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$ although $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.
Thus the linear OLS coefficient can be reversed by non-linear propensity and baseline mean, with no parametric restriction on $m_0$ or $p$.

Colleagues 1,5,6,7,12 argue for positivity in Case 3 using $D-E[D|X]$ and the weighted average $E[h(X)Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$. That is the sign of the non-parametric residual, not the OLS residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. The split in the round is exactly this confusion between conditioning non-parametrically vs linear projection. With the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond binary D and continuous Y”, $E[Y|X]$ and $p(X)$ can be arbitrarily non-linear, so the linear projection does not preserve the sign.

Current best belief: Case 1 must be positive; Case 2 can be negative; Case 3 can be negative for a linear regression of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. Hence only Case 1 is sign-guaranteed. The E camp relies on an implicit linearity/non-parametric control assumption that is not permitted.

reflection_text.11:
The maintained potential-outcome model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. For binary $D$ $\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign preserving.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ the crude mean difference can be negative e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the $Y\sim1+D$ slope is not guaranteed positive.

Case 3: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population OLS is the linear projection on $1,D,X$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$,
$a=E[D]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$.  Write $r_{p}(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $w(X)=r_{p}(X)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]+E[r_{p}(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X)Var(D|X)]$.
The second term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$. The first term $E[r_{p}(X)m(X)]$ is the linear covariance of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity. With no parametric restriction on $m$ and $p$ this can be made arbitrarily negative.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r_{p}=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m(X)=-K\,r_{p}(X)$. 4.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.,

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;
h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0,$$

under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

* Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
For a binary $D$ the population OLS on $1,D$ is the mean difference

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0 .$$

Unconditional randomisation is sign preserving.

* Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$, $D\not\perp X$.
$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].$$
The selection term can dominate.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$,
$\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
The crude $Y\sim1+D$ slope can be $<0$.

* Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken.  Put
$\tilde D=D-a-bX$ with $a=E[D]-bE[X]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$ and
$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D\mid X]$. Then

$$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E\!\left[h(X)Var(D\mid X)\right]
      +E\!\left[w(X)m_{0}(X)\right]+E\!\left[w(X)p(X)h(X)\right],$$

$$Var(\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)]+E[w(X)^{2}].$$

The first term is $>0$, but $E[w m_{0}]$ is the linear covariance of the
baseline mean with the part of the propensity not linearly explained by
$X$.  With no parametric restriction $w(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is
non-linear in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w$.
E.g. $X=0,1,2$ $P(X)=1/3$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8,\;p(1)=0.2$ so $a=0.6,b=0$,
$w=(0.2,-0.4,0.2)$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$. Then
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall X$ but

$$\beta_{D}= \frac{E[h\,Var(D\mid X)]+E[w m_{0}]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]+E[w^{2}]}
        \propto 1-K/3<0$$

for $K>3$.  The non-parametric partial effect
$E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ is the coefficient on
$D-E[D\mid X]$, not on the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Without linearity of $m_{0}$ and $p$ the linear projection on $1,X$ does
not partial out $X$ non-parametrically and the sign can be reversed.

Hence with the stated no-parametric restriction a strictly positive
individual effect forces a positive population OLS slope only under
unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed.

A. Only Case 1.

under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign
reversed.  That is

With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., conditional unconfoundedness is

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ , $m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,
$p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.

The $1+D$ OLS is the mean difference, strictly positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
= E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$.

The selection term $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $\tau>0$ a.s.
The marginal $1+D$ regression can be Simpson reversed.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$.
With $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $E[\tilde D]=E[\tilde D X]=0$,
$w(X)=E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-a-bX$,

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]+E[w(X)\{m(X)+p(X)h(X)\}]$.

The first term is $>0$, the second is $E[w(X)m(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
$w(X)\neq0$ as soon as $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, and $m(X)$ can be
chosen anti-correlated with $w(X)$.  With $X\in\{0,1,2\}$,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$,
$h\equiv1$, $m(X)=-K\,w(X)$, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$
for every $X$, but

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)\propto E[h{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]+E[w m]
=0.24-0.08K$,

so $\beta_{D}<0$ for $K>3$.
The non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ gives
$E[h(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the $D-E[D\mid X]$
coefficient. The OLS residual is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, which is orthogonal
to $1,X$ only linearly, not to arbitrary functions of $X$.  With no
parametric linearity of $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the linear $1+D+X$
coefficient can be reversed.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS slope on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed
under $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and no further parametric restriction.

A. Only Case 1.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I am landing on E, only Case 1 and Case 3 are sign protected.

Under conditional unconfoundedness $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ we have

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and $h(X)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}\mid X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

So for every $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$:

$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=h(X)>0$.

Case 1 is uncontroversial. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ the intercept-slope OLS is exactly that mean difference.

Case 2 is the usual Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ the marginal means integrate over different $X$ distributions,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=E\{E[Y(1)\mid X]\mid D=1\}$, $E[Y\mid D=0]=E\{E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0\}$,
so $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term can dominate the positive $h$ term when $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ is monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. The $X\in\{0,1\}$ example with $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ is a clean instance where the crude $1+D$ regression is negative despite $\tau>0$ a.s.

Case 3 removes that composition bias. Write $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ and $\eta=D-p(X)$, $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Then

$E[Y\eta\mid X]=E[m_{0}(X)\eta\mid X]+E[D h(X)\eta\mid X]=h(X)E[D\eta\mid X]=h(X)Var(D\mid X)$,

because $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Hence

$Cov(Y,\eta)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]>0$, $Var(\eta)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$,

and the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$ part is

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\eta)/Var(\eta)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]$,

a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average effects $h(X)>0$ with weights $w(X)\propto Var(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$. The Frisch-Waugh residualisation makes the variation in $D$ used for estimation mean independent of $X$, so any function of $X$, in particular $m_{0}(X)$, is orthogonal to the residualised treatment variation. What remains is the within-$X$ monotone relationship $E[Y\mid X,D]$ increasing in $D$.

The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ hinge on identifying the OLS residual with $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ and then engineering $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$ where $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. That is a knife-edge construction where the baseline mean is chosen to be perfectly anti-correlated with the misspecification of the propensity relative to the linear span $\{1,X\}$. In the usual conditioning interpretation “controlling for $X$” means removing all $X$-related variation from $D$, i.e. working with $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is orthogonal to any function of $X$ by construction. Under that partialling out the coefficient is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted mean of the strictly positive $h(X)$.

So unconditional randomisation guarantees a positive slope, conditional randomisation does not guarantee a positive marginal slope, and conditional randomisation does guarantee a positive slope once $X$ is included in the regression. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the A bloc on Case 1 and on the sign problem in Case 2, and I think that is exactly why Case 3 is sign protected.

Case 1. D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1). Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=Eτ>0 for every realisation of τ>0 a.s., so the intercept–slope regression of Y on 1,D is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1)|X but D is correlated with X marginally. With Y=Y0+Dτ,
E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D h(X) with m0(X)=E[Y0|X] and h(X)=E[τ|X]>0 a.s. Hence
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The selection term E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0] is unrestricted. With p(X)=E[D|X] decreasing in X while m0(X) is increasing, the composition effect dominates. The X∈{0,1}, Y0=100X, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 example gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0] despite τ>0 a.s. So the crude regression Y~1+D is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now condition on X. Let p(X)=E[D|X] and r=D-p(X). Then E[r|X]=0 and conditional unconfoundedness gives
E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D h(X), h(X)>0 a.s.

Cov(Y,r)=E[ Cov(Y,r|X) ] =E[ Cov(m0(X)+D h(X),r|X) ] =E[ h(X) Cov(D,r|X) ] because E[r|X]=0 implies Cov(m0(X),r|X)=0.
Since Cov(D,r|X)=Var(D|X)=p(X)(1-p(X)),
Cov(Y,r)=E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] >0.

Var(r)=E[Var(D|X)]>0 on the support where 0<p(X)<1. Hence in the population the coefficient on D in the regression of Y on 1,D,X, i.e. the Frisch-Waugh coefficient on the part of D orthogonal to X, is

βD = Cov(Y,r)/Var(r)= E[ h(X)Var(D|X) ] / E[ Var(D|X) ] = Σx w(x)h(x)

with w(x)=Var(D|X=x)/E[Var(D|X)]≥0, Σw=1. This is a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average treatment effects h(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]>0. Controlling for X removes the composition bias that flips the sign in Case 2, and the residualised variation in D is mean independent of X so any function of X, in particular m0(X), is orthogonal to r.

Thus the population partial effect is the average of strictly positive conditional gains. Positivity is guaranteed for the unconditionally randomised regression and for the regression that includes X, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$, but
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)=E[D|X]$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ is increasing, the selection term can dominate the positive gain. The $Y_{0}=100X,\ \tau\equiv1,\ p(0)=0.9,\ p(1)=0.1$ example does exactly that. The crude $Y\sim1+D$ slope is not sign protected.

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s. and
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta m_{0}(X)]+E[\eta D h(X)]
=E[h(X)E[\eta D|X]]=E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0,
$$
because $E[\eta|X]=0$ makes $\eta$ orthogonal to any function of $X$, in particular to $m_{0}(X)$. With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$,
$$
\beta_{D}^{X}= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)}{\operatorname{Var}(\eta)}
     =\frac{E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}
     =\sum_{x} w(x) h(x),
$$
a convex weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average effects $h(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]$ with weights $w(x)\propto \operatorname{Var}(D|X=x)=p(x)(1-p(x))>0$.
That is the Frisch-Waugh form of the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$-predictable part of $D$. Intuitively, once pre-treatment income $X$ is held fixed the remaining variation in program participation is mean independent of $X$ and $E[Y|X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. With $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. the $X$-residualised variation in $Y$ remains positively correlated with the $X$-residualised variation in $D$, so the population partial effect is $>0$.

Hence positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and, once $X$ is included in the regression, under conditional randomisation, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I am landing on E, only Case 1 and Case 3 are sign protected.

Under conditional unconfoundedness $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ we have

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and $h(X)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}\mid X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

So for every $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$:

$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=h(X)>0$.

Case 1 is uncontroversial. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ the intercept-slope OLS is exactly that mean difference.

Case 2 is the usual Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ the marginal means integrate over different $X$ distributions,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=E\{E[Y(1)\mid X]\mid D=1\}$, $E[Y\mid D=0]=E\{E[Y(0)\mid X]\mid D=0\}$,
so $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[h(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term can dominate the positive $h$ term when $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ is monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. The $X\in\{0,1\}$ example with $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ is a clean instance where the crude $1+D$ regression is negative despite $\tau>0$ a.s.

Case 3 removes that composition bias. Write $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ and $\eta=D-p(X)$, $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Then

$E[Y\eta\mid X]=E[m_{0}(X)\eta\mid X]+E[D h(X)\eta\mid X]=h(X)E[D\eta\mid X]=h(X)Var(D\mid X)$,

because $E[\eta\mid X]=0$. Hence

$Cov(Y,\eta)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]>0$, $Var(\eta)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$,

and the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$ part is

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\eta)/Var(\eta)=E[h(X)Var(D\mid X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]$,

a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average effects $h(X)>0$ with weights $w(X)\propto Var(D\mid X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$. The Frisch-Waugh residualisation makes the variation in $D$ used for estimation mean independent of $X$, so any function of $X$, in particular $m_{0}(X)$, is orthogonal to the residualised treatment variation. What remains is the within-$X$ monotone relationship $E[Y\mid X,D]$ increasing in $D$.

The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ hinge on identifying the OLS residual with $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ and then engineering $m_{0}(X)=-K\,w(X)$ where $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. That is a knife-edge construction where the baseline mean is chosen to be perfectly anti-correlated with the misspecification of the propensity relative to the linear span $\{1,X\}$. In the usual conditioning interpretation “controlling for $X$” means removing all $X$-related variation from $D$, i.e. working with $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is orthogonal to any function of $X$ by construction. Under that partialling out the coefficient is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted mean of the strictly positive $h(X)$.

So unconditional randomisation guarantees a positive slope, conditional randomisation does not guarantee a positive marginal slope, and conditional randomisation does guarantee a positive slope once $X$ is included in the regression. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D h(X) with m0(X)=E[Y0|X] and h(X)=E[τ|X]>0 a.s. Hence
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The selection term E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0] is unrestricted. With p(X)=E[D|X] decreasing in X while m0(X) is increasing, the composition effect dominates. The X∈{0,1}, Y0=100X, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 example gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0] despite τ>0 a.s. So the crude regression Y~1+D is not sign protected.

E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D h(X), h(X)>0 a.s.

Cov(Y,r)=E[ Cov(Y,r|X) ] =E[ Cov(m0(X)+D h(X),r|X) ] =E[ h(X) Cov(D,r|X) ] because E[r|X]=0 implies Cov(m0(X),r|X)=0.
Since Cov(D,r|X)=Var(D|X)=p(X)(1-p(X)),
Cov(Y,r)=E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] >0.

Var(r)=E[Var(D|X)]>0 on the support where 0<p(X)<1. Hence in the population the coefficient on D in the regression of Y on 1,D,X, i.e. the Frisch-Waugh coefficient on the part of D orthogonal to X, is

βD = Cov(Y,r)/Var(r)= E[ h(X)Var(D|X) ] / E[ Var(D|X) ] = Σx w(x)h(x)

with w(x)=Var(D|X=x)/E[Var(D|X)]≥0, Σw=1. This is a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average treatment effects h(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]>0. The classic X∈{0,1}, Y0=100X, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. The marginal Y~1+D regression is not sign protected. That is the usual Simpson reversal.

Case 3 is different. Under D ⊥ Y(0),Y(1)|X
E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D h(X), h(X)>0 a.s.
so for every X the conditional mean is strictly increasing in D. Let p(X)=E[D|X] and η=D-p(X). Then E[η|X]=0 and

Cov(Y,η)=E[η m0(X)]+E[η D h(X)] = E[ h(X) E[ D η|X ] ] = E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] >0,

because E[η|X]=0 kills the m0 term and E[D η|X]=Var(D|X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0 on the support. With Var(η)=E[Var(D|X)]>0

β_D = Cov(Y,η)/Var(η)=E[ h(X) Var(D|X) ] / E[ Var(D|X) ].

That is a strictly positive weighted average of the conditional average effects h(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]>0 with weights w(X)∝Var(D|X). Up to the usual Frisch-Waugh re-scaling this is the population coefficient on D in the regression of Y on 1,D,X: after partialling out X the residual variation in D is mean independent of X and of any function of X, and E[Y|X,D] is monotone in D for every X. Controlling for pre-treatment income therefore removes the composition bias that flips the sign in Case 2 and the partial effect is the average of the strictly positive conditional gains.

The non-linear p(X) constructions that are quoted as reversing the sign in Case 3 rely on identifying “control for X” with the linear residual D-a-bX and then choosing m0(X) to be perfectly anti-correlated with the linear approximation error w(X)=p(X)-a-bX. That is a knife-edge correlation between the baseline mean function and the part of the propensity score that is not linear in X. Once X is partialled out non-parametrically, i.e. with the residual D-E[D|X] which is orthogonal to any function of X, the E[w m0] term disappears and the coefficient is the Var(D|X)-weighted mean above. In the usual conditioning interpretation of “regressing on X” the residual is D-E[D|X], not D-Proj_{1,X}D, and the sign is preserved.

Hence positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and under conditional randomisation once X is included in the regression, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.
public_text.12:
I think we are all agreed on the two extremes and the disagreement is really just Case 3.

Case 1 is uncontroversial. With unconditional randomisation $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$, 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E\tau>0$, so the intercept-slope regression of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and the population slope is strictly $>0$.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson reversal. Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$ for every $X$, but
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)=E[D|X]$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ is increasing, the selection term can dominate the positive gain. The $Y_{0}=100X,\ \tau\equiv1,\ p(0)=0.9,\ p(1)=0.1$ example does exactly that. The crude $Y\sim1+D$ slope is not sign protected.

Case 3 is different. Write $p(X)=E[D|X]$ and $\eta=D-p(X)$, so $E[\eta|X]=0$. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)>0$ a.s. and
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)=E[\eta m_{0}(X)]+E[\eta D h(X)]
=E[h(X)E[\eta D|X]]=E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0,
$$
because $E[\eta|X]=0$ makes $\eta$ orthogonal to any function of $X$, in particular to $m_{0}(X)$. With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$,
$$
\beta_{D}^{X}= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\eta)}{\operatorname{Var}(\eta)}
     =\frac{E[h(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]}
     =\sum_{x} w(x) h(x),
$$
a convex weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average effects $h(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]$ with weights $w(x)\propto \operatorname{Var}(D|X=x)=p(x)(1-p(x))>0$.
That is the Frisch-Waugh form of the population partial effect of $D$ after removing the $X$-predictable part of $D$. Intuitively, once pre-treatment income $X$ is held fixed the remaining variation in program participation is mean independent of $X$ and $E[Y|X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. Controlling for $X$ removes the composition bias that flips the sign in Case 2 and the regression coefficient is the $Var(D|X)$-weighted mean of the positive conditional gains.

The non-linear $p(X)$ constructions that are quoted as making the $1+D+X$ slope negative rely on identifying the OLS residual with $D-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}D$ and then choosing $m_{0}(X)$ to be perfectly anti-correlated with the linear approximation error $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$. That is a knife-edge tuning of the baseline mean function to the non-linear part of the propensity. In the usual conditioning interpretation the residual that is partialled out is $D-E[D|X]$, which is by construction orthogonal to every function of $X$. With $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. the $X$-residualised variation in $Y$ remains positively correlated with the $X$-residualised variation in $D$, so the population partial effect is $>0$.

Hence positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and, once $X$ is included in the regression, under conditional randomisation, but not for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$. For binary $D$ the population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly the mean difference, so the $D$ coefficient is strictly positive. Uncontroversial.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate the positive $h$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$ regression can be negative. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,8 agree; colleagues 1,12,5,7 claim positivity is preserved, which conflates conditional positivity with marginal positivity.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[r]=E[rX]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[r(X)m(X)]+E[r(X)p(X)h(X)]+E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]$.
The last term $E[h{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial covariance.
The first term $E[r(X)m(X)]$ is the linear partial covariance of $p(X)$ with $m(X)$. With no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $r(X)$ can be non-zero when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m(X)$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $r(X)$ to make the covariance arbitrarily negative.

Explicit counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $r=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m(X)=-K\,r(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, but ${\rm Cov}(\tilde D,Y)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$. The same construction with $p(X)=X^{2}$ and $m(X)=-K\big(p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ yields negative OLS coefficient while the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Hence the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives
$\beta^{np}=E[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the argument used by colleagues 1,12,5,6,7,9 for option E. It is correct for the non-parametric partial effect but not for the linear projection $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ actually estimated by $Y\sim1+D+X$. The sign reversal requires only non-linearity of $p(X)$ in $X$, which is allowed under “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”.

Thus positivity of $\tau_i>0$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed. Current belief: Only Case 1 must be positive, option A. The disagreement in the round is exactly the confusion between $D-E[D|X]$ orthogonality to any function of $X$ and $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ orthogonality only to $1,X$.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The maintained potential-outcomes model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. For binary $D$ $\beta_D=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$. The intercept-slope OLS is the ATE, sign forced.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. Marginal mean difference is 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing the selection term can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. All sides agree.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$.
$\beta_D=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$, $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Write $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $>0$. The $E[w m_0]$ term is the linear covariance of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity. With no parametric restriction on $m_0$ and $p$, $w\neq0$ when $p$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m_0$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w$.

Example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}p\equiv0.6$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0(X)=-K w(X)$. With the non-parametric residual $\eta=D-p(X)$, $E[\eta|X]=0$, 
$Cov(Y,\eta)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and $\beta^{np}=E[h Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$, a $Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the correct partial effect after non-parametric partialling out of $X$. The E-camp interprets “controlling for X” as that non-parametric residual and claims Case 3 is sign preserved.

With the literal linear regression stated in the problem, the residual is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given” $m_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ can be non-linear, so $E[w m_0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative and reverse the sign. Hence Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed.

Persistent disagreement in round 2 is exactly this linear vs non-parametric interpretation of “regress Y on 1,D,X”. Current best reading under the literal linear OLS formulation is sign guaranteed only for unconditional randomisation.

Current belief: Only Case 1, option A. Unresolved is whether the question intends linear projection or non-parametric control for $X$; the E-camp maintains the latter interpretation.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The maintained structure is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., so under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. For binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$.
Unconditional randomisation forces a positive mean difference and the intercept-slope OLS is that difference. Sign guaranteed.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ marginally.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$, $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w m_{0}]$ is the linear covariance of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity. With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}$ and $p$, $w\neq0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m_{0}$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w$. Example $X=0,1,2$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8,p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6,b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$.

The $E[hVar(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ expression is the coefficient on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, which is orthogonal to any function of $X$. OLS with a linear control for $X$ uses the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D|X]$. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ the linear control does not partial out arbitrary functions of $X$ and the sign can reverse.

Hence a strictly positive $\tau_i$ forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation.

Disagreement in the group is whether “regress Y on 1,D,X’’ should be interpreted as the linear projection or as partialling out $X$ non-parametrically, i.e. the $Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 argue for the latter and claim Case 3 is sign-preserved, giving answer E. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 argue the OLS residual is linear and give examples above showing sign reversal, giving answer A.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes setup is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Binary $D$, OLS is the linear projection.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$ unconditionally. $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E\tau>0$. Sign forced. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$. Marginal $1+D$ slope is $\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, the crude mean difference can be negative. Example $X\in\{0,1\}, Y_0=100X, \tau\equiv1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Case 3. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$, linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $a=E[D], b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

First term $>0$. The second term is the linear covariance of $m_0$ with the non-linear part of the propensity. If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w\neq0$, and $m_0$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w$ to make $E[w m_0]$ arbitrarily negative while keeping $h>0$. Example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8,p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6,b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_0(X)=-K w(X)$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ $\forall X$ but $\beta_D\propto1-K<0$ for $K>1$. The OLS residual is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not $D-E[D|X]$. Without linearity of $m_0$ and $p$, the linear control does not partial out $X$ non-parametrically and sign can reverse.

The split in the room is exactly this: colleagues 1,5,7,12, etc. argue for E, identifying control for $X$ with the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ and claiming $\beta_D=E[h Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 argue for A, pointing out the OLS residual is $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ and the $E[w m_0]$ term is unrestricted under the stated no-parametric restriction.

Given the problem explicitly says "Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given", the linear projection interpretation is the correct one, so Cases 2 and 3 can both be sign reversed while keeping $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1\mid X$.

Current belief: positivity guaranteed only in Case 1, i.e. option A. Cases 2 and 3 are not sign protected under the stated no-parametric restriction.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. under $D\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1. $D\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E\tau>0$ and for binary $D$ the population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is exactly that mean difference. Positivity is forced. Unanimous.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ despite $\tau>0$ a.s. The marginal $1+D$ slope can be negative. Unanimous.

$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcome structure is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $h(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $m_{0}$ increasing and $p$ decreasing the marginal mean difference can be negative despite $h>0$ a.s. The $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ example gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. All colleagues agree Case 2 is not sign protected.

Case 3 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ is taken.
Frisch-Waugh: $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$, $a=E[D]$, $b=Cov(D,X)/Var(X)$.
Let $w(X)=E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[h(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)h(X)]$.
The first term $E[hVar(D|X)]>0$. The second term $E[w m_{0}]$ is the linear covariance of the baseline mean with the non-linear part of the propensity. With no parametric restriction on $m_{0}$ and $p$, $w\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $m_{0}$ can be chosen anti-correlated with $w$ arbitrarily.

Explicit sign reversal: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.8$, $p(1)=0.2$, $a=0.6$, $b=0$, $w=0.2,-0.4,0.2$, $h\equiv1$, $m_{0}(X)=-K w(X)$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)=(1-K/3)$ $ <0$ for $K>3$. 
The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[h Var(D|X)]>0$ and $\beta^{np}=E[h Var(D|X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$, a $Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$. That is the sign the E-camp quotes. It is the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.

With the usual linear OLS interpretation and no linearity imposed on $m_{0}$ or $p$, the linear projection does not preserve the sign. Hence a strictly positive individual effect forces a positive population OLS slope only under unconditional randomisation.
